_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a2.1: Rabbi Yishmael says: a maidservant: a full-fledged one.
rashi:a2.2: All those with whom relations are forbidden are enumerated: [all of them] are free women, and we have no exception; and this one is certainly different: she is half-maidservant and half-free woman.
rashi:a4.1: Gemara. She shall be [subjected] to the reciting: for they recite over her: “Then the Lord will make your plagues extraordinary” (Deuteronomy 28:59), as they recite over those who are flogged, in tractate Makkot (22b).
rashi:a4.2: She shall be subject to an assessment: for if she cannot withstand forty [lashes], they assess her by examination and reckoning.
rashi:a4.3: Lashes fit to be divided by three: for example eighteen, or twenty-one, or twenty-four, for they would strike him two parts (in front of him and one behind him) [so the text reads; the mishna in Makkot 22b has one third in front and two thirds behind], and we derive it from a verse in tractate Makkot (23a).
rashi:a5.1: At the time that the woman is flogged: that she is an adult and subject to punishment.
rashi:a7.1: Say that the verse excludes him: [the Gemara] goes back to the mishna, which teaches that [the Torah] did not equate the woman with the man with regard to an offering. Say that the verse excludes him from lashes, as it is written “there shall be” [in the feminine]; but as for her, say that she is flogged and brings an offering.
rashi:a8.1: It is a term of change: that she has changed from her natural state.
rashi:a8.2: Groats [harifot]: something that has changed through pounding; and here too [she has changed] through the male organ in intercourse.
rashi:a9.1: And they gave their hand that they would divorce: it is a verse in the book of Ezra.
rashi:a11.1: Redeemed [and not redeemed]: “and not at all redeemed” [vehofdeh lo nifdata] implies redeemed and not redeemed.
rashi:a13.1: According to Rabbi Yishmael, from where does he derive betrothed to a Hebrew slave: Granted, according to Rabbi Akiva, who establishes [the verse] as one who is half free, no verse is needed, for one can say: since the Merciful One rendered [the man] liable for her, she is certainly betrothed to a Jew, as betrothal takes effect with her. Therefore one can say that she was betrothed to a Hebrew slave, for his master gives her to him even against his will, as is explained in Kiddushin (14b), and not to a Canaanite slave, for she is forbidden to him. But according to Rabbi Yishmael, who says she is a full-fledged maidservant, from where does he derive [that she is] betrothed to a Hebrew slave? (The printed text adds here, in parentheses: “that he says to a Hebrew slave, since she is forbidden to him.”) Perhaps [she is betrothed] to a Canaanite slave, since according to him she is entirely permitted [to a Canaanite slave], more so than to a Hebrew one.
rashi:a15.1: If it is not needed for the matter of her: for it is [already] written: “And not at all redeemed” (Leviticus 19:20).
rashi:a16.1: Mishna. All those with whom relations are forbidden: if one of them is an adult, whether the man or the woman, the one is liable and the other exempt; and with the maidservant it is not so, and the Gemara explains it.
rashi:a16.2: Unwitting with a sin offering and intentional with karet: and with the maidservant, granted that if he acted intentionally and she unwittingly they are exempt, since she is not flogged, as we said above: “There shall be an inspection… and he shall bring his guilt offering,” and if not, they are exempt. But if he acted unwittingly and she intentionally, she is [liable] to lashes and he to a guilt offering, as we say in this chapter that the unwitting and the intentional are equal for one who has intercourse with the maidservant.
rashi:a17.1: Gemara. And here a minor is liable: asked in astonishment: is a minor liable with the maidservant?
rashi:a17.2: For they are juxtaposed to each other: as we said above: if the woman is not flogged, the man does not bring a guilt offering.
rashi:a18.1: And is one who is sleeping liable: asked in astonishment.
rashi:a20.1: One who engages in the initial stage is not liable: for “lies carnally [shikhvat zera]” is written with regard to her.
rashi:a20.2: If she intended it, she is liable, and if not, she is not liable: for we require “lies carnally [shikhvat zera],” and one who does not intend, for example one who fell from a roof and was thrust in, is not fit to inseminate.
rashi:a22.1: And if he teaches it with regard to the other forbidden relations, it should teach the opposite: [that] they rendered one who engages in the initial stage with forbidden relations liable like one who completes, [and] atypical [intercourse] liable like typical, for “the lyings of a woman” [mishkevei isha] is written (Leviticus 19 [as printed]).
tosafot:a4.1: She shall be [subjected] to the readings: This is puzzling: for [nowhere] is it explained that one must recite at the time that one flogs, if not from here.
tosafot:a5.1: The woman is not flogged: for example, where she acted unwittingly or is a minor, the man does not bring an offering. And as for what we say, “to include the unwitting like the intentional,” that means the man’s unwitting [act] is like [his] intentional one; but the woman must have acted intentionally.
tosafot:a12.1: Betrothed to a Canaanite slave: not precisely, for betrothal does not take effect with her.
tosafot:a13.1: And according to Rabbi Yishmael, granted “and not at all redeemed,” etc., the Torah spoke in the language of people: And so too it says in the Jerusalem Talmud: they are doubled expressions, and the Torah spoke with them: “you have gone, you have gone [halokh halakhta],” “you longed, you longed [nikhsof nikhsafta],” “I was indeed stolen [gunov gunavti]”; and Rabbi Akiva disagrees. And everywhere that it says: “This works out well according to the one who says the Torah spoke in the language of people, but according to the one who says, etc.,” that is Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva.
tosafot:a17.1: For they are juxtaposed to each other: The wording is not precise, for the man is juxtaposed to the woman, but the woman is not juxtaposed to the man; for [even] when the man [is a minor], the woman is liable, as is stated in the Torat Kohanim: “And a man” excludes a minor. Might I think that I exclude [even] a boy of nine years and one day? The verse states: “And a man.” If so, the woman is not juxtaposed to the man.
tosafot:a19.1: With one who does not intend (typical), he is exempt: The Kuntres [Rashi] explained: because “lies carnally [shikhvat zera]” is written, and one who does not intend is not fit to inseminate, for example one who fell from a roof and was thrust in. But this is difficult: who tells us that he is not fit to inseminate? Rather, the reason is that he is a victim of circumstance [anus].
gershom:a1.1: [An editor’s marker notes that what precedes belongs to 10b.] She shall be [subjected] to the readings: to the reciting, as we learned: The greatest of the judges recites at the time of the flogging: “If you will not observe to do… then the Lord will make your plagues extraordinary” (Deuteronomy 28:58–59).
gershom:a2.1: She shall be subject to an assessment: by estimate; that is flogging, as we learned: One assesses him only, etc.
gershom:a3.1: At the time that the woman is flogged: where she is an adult and he is an adult, the man brings an offering.
gershom:a4.1: The woman is not flogged: where she is a minor, the man does not bring an offering, even though he is an adult.
gershom:a5.1: Since until here: [up to] “nor was freedom given her,” the verse speaks about the man: “A man who lies carnally with a woman”; let it write first, etc.
gershom:a6.1: This is what it is saying: If there will be an inspection: that she is an adult, [the act was] in the typical manner, and she intended.
gershom:a7.1: He shall bring his guilt offering: when she is [subject] to the inspection.
gershom:a8.1: And say that he: is not flogged, for the verse excluded him: “There shall be an inspection,” she and not he.
gershom:a9.1: “He shall bring his guilt offering” is written: and not “she shall bring her guilt offering.”
gershom:a10.1: Actually, he is liable to an offering only for a non-virgin maidservant: who had intercourse before that.
gershom:a11.1: Designated [ḥarufa]: like groats [harifot], which have changed from their original [state].
gershom:a12.1: Though you should bray: for she has already been pounded through intercourse and changed, like groats.
gershom:a13.1: To divorce their wives: the foreign women, in the days of Ezra.
gershom:a14.1: They had intercourse with espoused maidservants: for which one is liable to a ram as a guilt offering.
gershom:a15.1: Rabbi Yishmael says: This is a certain maidservant: who is not redeemed at all.
gershom:a16.1: All those with whom relations are forbidden are enumerated: in the Torah, how one is liable for them. We have no exception that was not made explicit in the Torah except this alone: that for one who is half-maidservant and half-free woman one is liable, and not for another [maidservant]. And Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya is [the same as] Rabbi Akiva, as is said in the Gemara below.
gershom:a17.1: If “not redeemed,” I might think that she was not redeemed at all; the verse states: “And she was redeemed.”
gershom:a18.1: And betrothed to a Hebrew slave: for it is written: “Designated [neḥerefet] for a man,” and ḥarufa is also a term of betrothal, as it says in tractate Kiddushin [an editor suggests reading: one who says “my ḥarufa,” she is betrothed]: “my ḥarufa” ([a variant:] “my designated”). [That she is] betrothed to a Jew cannot be said, for since she is half-maidservant she is forbidden to a Jew; but a Hebrew slave is permitted both to a Canaanite maidservant and to a Jewish woman.
gershom:a19.1: The Torah spoke in the language of people: [meaning] that she was not redeemed at all.
gershom:a20.1: Granted according to Rabbi Yishmael, etc.: Granted according to Rabbi Akiva, it is not necessary [an editor suggests reading: a verse is not necessary for this, for necessarily it speaks of a Hebrew slave, since being half free she is fit to marry only a Hebrew slave] to say it, for it does not teach us a novelty, since being half free she is fit to marry a Hebrew slave. But according to Rabbi Yishmael, why a Hebrew slave? Because it is written: “Because she was not free”; by inference, he is free: he is not Canaanite but Hebrew.
gershom:a21.1: In general I hold in accordance with you, that the Torah spoke in the language of people: as we say [about] “shall utterly be cut off [hikkaret tikkaret]”: Rabbi Elazar said: The Torah spoke in the language of people. And here it is different, for since, etc.
gershom:a22.1: If it is not needed for the matter of her: this “because she was not free,” for it is [already] written: “And not at all redeemed,” apply it to the matter of him: that he is not free, that is, he is Canaanite.
gershom:a23.1: One is an adult and one is a minor: either the male or the female.
gershom:a24.1: A minor is exempt: and for one who has intercourse with an espoused maidservant, is a minor liable? Asked in astonishment: why [would he be]?
gershom:a25.1: And here, with an espoused maidservant, the adult is also exempt when she is a minor. What is the reason? For they are juxtaposed to each other, as we said above: “If there will be an inspection,” she; “and he shall bring his guilt offering,” he.
gershom:a26.1: One who completes with a maidservant is liable: for there is “lying carnally [shikhvat zera]” at the completion of intercourse.
gershom:a27.1: [If] she intends, [they are] liable: both she and he.
gershom:a28.1: What is the reason? “Lies carnally [shikhvat zera]” is written: and she does not conceive except through typical [intercourse].
gershom:a29.1: And furthermore, if you teach it with regard to a maidservant, awake like sleeping, what is that? Is it not the same as intending like not intending? For one who is awake intends, and one who is sleeping does not intend.
rashi:b4.1: It is found that one who intends and engages in the initial stage with the maidservant: one who engaged in the initial stage with her intentionally is exempt, for the initial stage with the maidservant is exempt; [he is] like one who does not intend with forbidden relations. [What] the initial stage [is] is a matter of dispute (in Sanhedrin, in the chapter Arba Mitot, 55b): there is one who says the initial stage is the touching [lit. kissing] [of the organs], and there is one who says it is the insertion of the corona.
rashi:b6.1: Mishna. They said to him: it is explained in the Gemara.
rashi:b7.1: If [two] brought him, etc.: for example, if they testified about him that he killed a person.
rashi:b7.2: If he wishes to say: I acted intentionally: if he wished to exempt himself with a lie, he could say he acted intentionally, and one who acts intentionally is exempt [from an offering].
rashi:b12.1: Gemara. It is Rabbi Meir: who said: If two brought him, etc.
rashi:b13.1: What does it teach us? We learn it from the latter clause: which teaches: Two say he ate, etc.
rashi:b13.2: This is what it is saying: the latter clause [teaches that] this matter that we learned above, “They said to him: You ate, etc., he brings a sin offering,” is not the statement of all; rather, it is a dispute of Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis, for Rabbi Meir says: If two brought him, etc., and the Rabbis say, etc.; and the latter clause explains the first clause.
rashi:b14.1: Some say: the Gemara asks thus: “they said” implies even one, etc.
rashi:b15.1: She is permitted to return to him: to the first, and [this is] on the basis of witnesses, two of whom said to her: Your husband died. Therefore she is permitted to the first, for she acted under duress, since two said it to her, and [a wife who acted under] duress remains permitted to an Israelite [husband who is not a priest].
rashi:b16.1: By inference, the first clause: which teaches “she must leave this one and that one,” [is a case] where she married with the consent of the court and on the basis of one witness, for she should have investigated carefully whether he had died. For the reason the Rabbis permitted her to marry on the basis of one witness is that she investigates carefully and [only then] marries, since by the stringency you imposed on her at the end, that she must leave this one and that one, you were lenient with her at the beginning, as said in tractate Yevamot (88a). Therefore, [where] she married on the basis of one witness and did not herself investigate, and it turned out that he had not died, she must leave this one and that one, as we say in tractate Sota (27b): “And she was defiled… and she was defiled,” twice: once [forbidding her] to the husband and once to the paramour.
rashi:b19.1: Actually, where he does not contradict him: and our mishna teaches thus: “They said to him, etc.” In what case is this said? Where he is silent; but if he contradicts him, for example a witness said he ate and he said: I did not eat, he is exempt.
rashi:b20.1: Is known to him: implies of his own accord, and not that others inform him.
tosafot:b2.1: This is what it is teaching: they rendered, etc.: And this is the explanation of the baraita: they rendered one who completes like one who engages in the initial stage, and one who intends like one who does not intend, and this law is with typical and atypical [intercourse], as the Gemara explains. In any case it is slightly difficult: why did it not teach awake like sleeping together with them, but taught it after typical and atypical?
tosafot:b4.1: It is found that one who intends, etc.: It is difficult: why did the Gemara lengthen its language? For this is not an explanation of the baraita, since we have already concluded it well.
tosafot:b4.2: Like one who does not intend with forbidden relations: The Kuntres [Rashi] explained: for example, where his wife and his sister were in the bed, and he thought to have intercourse with his wife and it turned out to be his sister, where he is exempt from lashes and liable to a sin offering since he derived pleasure, for he is one who acts unawares [mitasek]. But this is difficult: for with the maidservant too he is liable to an offering in such a case, since one brings [the offering] for the intentional as for the unwitting [the Hebrew says “sin offering”; for the maidservant the mishna’s offering is a guilt offering]. If so, what does it mean: one who intends with the maidservant is found to be like one who does not intend with forbidden relations? In such a case the two are equal! Therefore one may say: like one who does not intend with forbidden relations, for example one who fell from a roof and was thrust in, who is entirely exempt, for he is a victim of circumstance.
tosafot:b6.1: Mishna. They said to him… a witness says: He ate, etc.: It must be that [the mishna] speaks where [the two] testified about him at the same time; for if one after the other, then wherever the Torah deemed one witness credible, he is [as good as] two, and once his testimony was accepted we no longer pay attention to the testimony of the second, who says: He did not eat. And it must be that it speaks where the man about whom they testify is silent; for if he said: I do not know, he is exempt, as is derived in the Gemara from “or if [his sin] is known to him,” etc. And [the Gemara] concludes that it speaks of one witness, who cannot render him liable to bring an offering, and necessarily it speaks where the one about whom he testified says: I do not know; for if he said: I did not eat, it is obvious that one witness is not credible, as it is written: “One witness shall not rise up against a man” (Deuteronomy 19:15), from which it appears that one witness rises only for an oath.
tosafot:b6.2: And a woman says: He did not eat: From here it is implied that a woman is more credible than a robber; for with regard to a robber it is implied that we do not say silence is like admission, as we say (Kiddushin 66a): “If he is credible to you that he is not a robber, go divorce her,” even though she was silent; evidently we do not say that silence is like admission. And the incident was: that blind man who would arrange mishnayot before Rav Sheshet, etc.; a certain man came and said that [the blind man’s] wife had committed adultery, and he said: If he is credible to you that he is not a robber, go divorce her. And here, if he is silent, the woman is believed.
tosafot:b6.3: A witness says: He ate, and he says: I did not eat, he is exempt: And the same is true if he said: I do not know, as I explained.
tosafot:b9.1: For if he ate half an olive-bulk and again ate half an olive-bulk from one type, he is liable; from two types, he is exempt: And if you say: But we say in the chapter Kodshei Mizbe’aḥ (Me’ila 17b): Piggul and notar do not combine, and it says in the Gemara: They taught this only with regard to impurity of the hands, but for eating they combine? One may say that there it is with regard to lashes; alternatively, with regard to where they fell into one pot, they combine to impart flavor, since it is one name, for there is only one prohibition for both; but here it speaks of the law of liability to an offering.
tosafot:b11.1: Say the middle clause: A witness says he ate, and he says: I did not eat, etc.: And the same is so, that it could have brought [the inference] from the first clause: A witness says he ate and a witness says he did not eat, and he brings a provisional guilt offering. The reason is that one witness said he did not eat; but otherwise he would be liable to a sin offering, for silence is like admission. For necessarily it speaks where he was silent, for if he contradicted him he would be entirely exempt, and even if he says: I do not know, as I explained.
tosafot:b12.1: Rather, where he contradicts them, and whose is it? It is Rabbi Meir: for one cannot say it speaks where he said: I do not know, since [then] it is obvious that he is liable, for “I do not know” in the face of two witnesses is like silence.
tosafot:b13.1: This matter is a dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis: It is puzzling: for what purpose was it necessary to state it anonymously in the first clause? If so that it should be an anonymous [ruling] followed by a dispute, it is obvious, for [between] an individual and the many, the halakha follows the many.
tosafot:b16.1: By inference, the first clause is with the consent of the court and one witness: for with two witnesses there is no need for the consent of the court.
gershom:b1.1: [An editor’s marker notes that what precedes belongs to 11a.] Should I remove it: this baraita, since there is no way to resolve it?
gershom:b2.1: They rendered one who completes atypical [intercourse] with a maidservant, etc.
gershom:b3.1: Like one who does not intend, in the typical manner, where she is exempt: for example, where he fell from a roof and was thrust in. And now [the Gemara] seeks to resolve it so as to compare it also to forbidden relations, [where one is] exempt. It is found that one who intends and engages in the initial stage with the maidservant intentionally, even in the typical manner, is exempt, like one who does not intend with forbidden relations, who is exempt; and that is [the meaning of] “they rendered one who intends like one who does not intend.” And likewise, one who does not intend, in the typical manner, with a maidservant is exempt; one sleeping, in the typical manner, with a maidservant is exempt, like one sleeping with forbidden relations, who is exempt, as we learned: [In] all [cases of] forbidden relations, one awake and one sleeping, the one sleeping is exempt.
gershom:b4.1: And it is found that one who is awake and completes atypical [intercourse] with a maidservant is exempt, like one sleeping with all forbidden relations. And the exemption with forbidden relations exists only [for] one who does not intend, as we said, and one who is sleeping; but one who intends atypical [intercourse] is liable with forbidden relations, for “lies carnally” is not written with regard to them. And now they resolve them all, “they rendered one who completes like one who engages in the initial stage,” [as comparisons] to the exemption of forbidden relations.
gershom:b6.1: They said to him, two [witnesses]: You ate forbidden fat: an olive-bulk, he brings a sin offering.
gershom:b7.1: A witness says: He ate, etc., he brings a provisional guilt offering: for it is uncertain, since they contradict each other. And in this a woman’s testimony is credible, for it is included in the Sifra from “or,” as it is written: “Or if [his sin] is known to him,” in any case.
gershom:b8.1: One witness says: He ate, and he says: I did not eat: he is exempt from an offering, for a person is believed about himself, in a matter that requires atonement, more than a hundred witnesses, for so we say in the Gemara that this is the view of the Rabbis; and all the more so here, where there is only one witness.
gershom:b9.1: If two brought him to death: for if they testified about him in a matter for which he is liable to death, they execute him on their word even though he contradicts them; shall they not bring him to an offering, which is lenient compared to death, even though he contradicts them?
gershom:b10.1: They said to him: No; rather, he is exempt, for this one who says “I did not eat” is not [really] contradicting them, for if he wishes he can say: I did not eat unwittingly but intentionally, and one who acts intentionally is exempt from an offering. And since he can say this, when he said “I did not eat,” he is exempt.
gershom:b11.1: But [if] he is silent, [when] silent to one [witness] he is liable to an offering, and all the more so when he is silent to two, that he is liable to an offering; and this we can infer from the middle clause, and the first clause did not need to be stated.
gershom:b12.1: Rather, where he contradicts them: in the first clause, and even so he brings a sin offering. And whose is it? Rabbi Meir’s, who says: [the] contradiction, etc.
gershom:b13.1: But according to the Rabbis he is exempt: that is the latter clause.
gershom:b14.1: Indeed so; but this is what the first clause teaches us: where he contradicts them, that this matter is the dispute of Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis in the latter clause. And [the second version] holds that [“they said”] is said even of one. “And [witnesses] came and said to her”: [if] she married without the consent of the court, for she did not need to take permission from the court, since she married on the basis of two witnesses, she is permitted to return to him; for she is not like one who had intercourse willingly, who is forbidden to her husband, but is like one who had intercourse under duress. For what more should she have investigated, after two witnesses said to her: Your husband died?
gershom:b15.1: By inference, the first clause, which teaches “she must leave this one and that one,” [is] where she married with consent, having had only one witness, and needed to take permission from the court to marry. And why is she forbidden to her husband? For she is like one who had intercourse willingly with another, since she should not have married except on the basis of two. Evidently this “and they said to her” of the first clause is one witness.
gershom:b16.1: After all, what does the first clause teach us? We learn it from the middle clause.
gershom:b17.1: Actually, where he does not contradict him [an editor suggests reading: and so it teaches: They said to him, etc. In what case is this said? Where he is silent; but if he contradicts him, it teaches in the middle clause that he is exempt]: as it teaches in the middle clause: exempt.
gershom:b18.1: As the Sages taught: “Or if [his sin] is known to him [hoda elav]”: it could have said “or if it is known to him [hoda lo],” which would imply that it was made known to him, that others informed him. What [is meant by] “hoda elav”? That the knowledge must be to him, that is, that he must recall it when they remind him; but if he contradicts him, he is exempt.
gershom:b19.1: And we say there in the Sifra: I might think that even [if] he does not contradict him but is silent, when one witness says to him: He ate forbidden fat, he would be exempt; the verse states: “Or if it is known,” in any case: whether by one witness, or by a relative, or by a woman, and he does not contradict him, he is liable.
